rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper consumer contradiction inside the launch: “A blood-pressure feature that needs a blood-pressure cuff to work.” A is strong, but “Whoop's clinical features are also a pitch to its next investors” turns valuation plus premium gating into a fundraising/exit read the update does not actually give you. B has one bad overclaim, but it does more to keep a founder out of fantasyland and closer to a reporter's real question.
gaps_in_A: “Whoop's clinical features are also a pitch to its next investors” overreaches; no current fundraising, investor appetite, or exit signal is supplied.
“ahead of a future round or exit” is speculation with a blazer on. The set admits it needs confirmation, but the angle headline already sold the thesis.
It misses the cleanest blood-pressure contradiction: the feature “requires a one-time calibration with a cuff” and is “not a diagnostic.” That is more concrete than the broader paywall critique.
“was designed to avoid that step” goes a little past the facts. The update says the blood-pressure feature is non-medical wellness, not that Whoop designed it specifically to avoid FDA clearance.
gaps_in_B: “a feature nobody has cleared” is not in the supplied facts. The update says competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG, not that nobody has cleared cuffless blood pressure.
“a company whose entire model is subscription rather than hardware margin” relies on outside knowledge, not the provided update.
“the feature they think they're paying for” assumes a user expectation the facts do not establish.
Next step “newsjack-detector” is slightly off for a live company launch. The first move should be proof collection and journalist fit-checking; detector only helps if you need an external news peg.
